title: Everybody created and stole: Armstrong from King Oliver
summary: Waters says musicians both create and borrow, citing Armstrong's debt to Oliver, his own six sessions with Oliver, and that he was always an alto player, not a real tenor man.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Yep, you see everybody created, you see what I mean? And then also everybody stole. For instance, Louis Armstrong was playing the trumpet before he was associated with King Oliver. But when he associated, got 'sociated with King Oliver directly, then he advanced in, and advanced in, from listening to King Oliver. But he was, at the end he played more than King Oliver because I - well I worked with King Oliver, 'cause at that period he wasn't playing as much as he did when he was young, see. But I still - Louis advanced from listening to King Oliver. His style is from King Oliver, that's obvious. When you record with King Oliver you have to play two choruses, which at that time that's all he could play - well that was in 1926 or '27. But first time that I recorded, the very first recordings which I made, 6 recordings with him, I made 36 numbers with King Oliver - the first recording I had when he came up, right away I could say "Well yeah, that's where Louis got his ideas". But Louis was playing more. See, so everybody creates and improves. See, but with me, I actually to tell you the truth, I actually was not a tenor player at all. I'm learning just now that I can (laughs) play a little tenor, you understand what I mean? But I've always been [an] alto player. See, because I was playing technical solos and things on the alto before I ever heard of a tenor, in a way of speaking.
